treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Complications indicating level 2 care include eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, haemorrhage, hyperkalaemia, severe oliguria, need for coagulation support or intravenous antihypertensive treatment, initial stabilisation of severe hypertension, evidence of cardiac failure, and abnormal neurology.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with pre-eclampsia for whom early birth is considered likely within 7 days.
decision_rules: Offer a course of antenatal corticosteroids in line with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth.

recommended_regimens.name: antenatal corticosteroids
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer when early birth is considered likely within 7 days.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with HELLP syndrome.
decision_rules: Do not use dexamethasone or betamethasone to treat HELLP syndrome.

not_recommended.name: dexamethasone
not_recommended.reason: Do not use to treat HELLP syndrome.

not_recommended.name: betamethasone
not_recommended.reason: Do not use to treat HELLP syndrome.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with hypertension during the postnatal period.
decision_rules: Offer enalapril and monitor maternal renal function and serum potassium.
Where possible, choose medicines taken once daily.
Adapt treatment to accommodate breastfeeding when the woman wishes to breastfeed.

recommended_regimens.name: enalapril
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer for postnatal hypertension with appropriate maternal monitoring.

response_assessment.timepoint: During enalapril treatment
response_assessment.method: Monitor maternal renal function and serum potassium.

supportive_care: Explain that antihypertensive treatment need not prevent breastfeeding and make treatment decisions with the woman according to her preferences.

For breastfed babies with symptoms of low blood pressure, particularly those born preterm, consider blood pressure monitoring during the first few weeks. Advise women after discharge to watch for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries or poor feeding.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Antihypertensive medicines can enter breast milk, but most result in very low milk levels and very small infant exposures unlikely to have clinical effects. The cited MHRA advice states that ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists are generally not recommended during breastfeeding but are not absolutely contraindicated when considered essential for the mother; careful infant follow-up for possible hypotension is recommended.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women of black African or Caribbean family origin with hypertension during the postnatal period.
decision_rules: Consider nifedipine, or consider amlodipine if it has previously controlled the woman's blood pressure successfully.

recommended_regimens.name: nifedipine
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider for postnatal hypertension in this population.

alternative_regimens.name: amlodipine
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider for postnatal hypertension in this population.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The woman has used it previously with successful blood pressure control.

supportive_care: When breastfeeding, consider monitoring symptomatic infants for low blood pressure during the first few weeks, particularly if born preterm, and advise observation for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries or poor feeding.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with postnatal hypertension whose blood pressure is not controlled by a single medicine.
decision_rules: Consider nifedipine or amlodipine combined with enalapril.
If that combination is ineffective or not tolerated, consider adding atenolol or labetalol, or replacing 1 existing medicine with atenolol or labetalol.

recommended_regimens.name: nifedipine and enalapril
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider combination treatment when a single medicine does not control postnatal blood pressure.

alternative_regimens.name: amlodipine and enalapril
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider as the other specified combination after inadequate control with one medicine.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: As an alternative to the nifedipine-containing combination.

alternative_regimens.name: atenolol
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider adding to the combination or replacing 1 medicine already in use.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The nifedipine or amlodipine plus enalapril combination is ineffective or not tolerated.

alternative_regimens.name: labetalol
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider adding to the combination or replacing 1 medicine already in use.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The nifedipine or amlodipine plus enalapril combination is ineffective or not tolerated.

response_assessment.timepoint: During postnatal antihypertensive treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess blood pressure control and treatment tolerability.
response_assessment.interpretation: Inadequate control with a single medicine prompts consideration of combination treatment; ineffective or poorly tolerated combination treatment prompts consideration of adding or substituting atenolol or labetalol.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Use medicines taken once daily when possible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with postnatal hypertension who are breastfeeding or expressing milk.
decision_rules: Where possible, avoid diuretics and angiotensin receptor blockers.
Explain that antihypertensive treatment can be adjusted to support breastfeeding.

not_recommended.name: diuretics
not_recommended.reason: Avoid where possible when treating postnatal hypertension during breastfeeding or milk expression.

not_recommended.name: angiotensin receptor blockers
not_recommended.reason: Avoid where possible when treating postnatal hypertension during breastfeeding or milk expression.

response_assessment.timepoint: During the first few weeks, if the baby has symptoms of low blood pressure
response_assessment.method: Consider monitoring the baby's blood pressure, particularly if born preterm.

supportive_care: On discharge, advise observation of the baby for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries and poor feeding.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited MHRA clarification allows a clinician to prescribe ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor antagonists during breastfeeding if treatment is considered essential for the mother; this does not remove the guideline's advice to avoid angiotensin receptor blockers where possible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Women with postnatal hypertension who are not breastfeeding and do not plan to breastfeed.
decision_rules: Treat according to the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This guideline does not specify a separate medicine sequence for this population.

document_sections.heading: Overview
document_sections.content: The guideline addresses diagnosis and management of hypertension, including pre-eclampsia, during pregnancy, labour and birth. It also covers care before conception for women with hypertension and care after a pregnancy affected by hypertension. Its aim is better care for women and babies.

document_sections.heading: Symptoms of pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: Advise pregnant women to seek immediate professional assessment for a severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, severe pain beneath the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Antiplatelet agents
document_sections.content: Advise pregnant women at high risk of pre-eclampsia to take aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth. High-risk features are hypertensive disease in an earlier pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and chronic hypertension. Give the same aspirin advice to women with more than 1 moderate risk factor: nulliparity, age 40 years or older, an interval between pregnancies of more than 10 years, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more at the first visit, a family history of pre-eclampsia, or multi-fetal pregnancy. [2010, amended 2019] At publication in June 2019, aspirin lacked UK marketing authorisation for this indication despite common clinical use. In England it must be prescribed rather than sold by a community pharmacy for prevention of pre-eclampsia; prescribers should consult the manufacturer's pregnancy advice.

document_sections.heading: Other pharmaceutical agents
document_sections.content: Do not use nitric oxide donors, progesterone, diuretics or low molecular weight heparin to prevent hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Nutritional supplements
document_sections.content: Do not recommend magnesium, folic acid, antioxidants (vitamins C and E), fish oils or algal oils, or garlic solely to prevent hypertensive disorders during pregnancy. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Diet
document_sections.content: Do not advise salt restriction during pregnancy solely as prevention of gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Lifestyle
document_sections.content: Give women with chronic hypertension or a risk of hypertensive disorders the same advice about rest, exercise and work as other healthy pregnant women. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Diabetes
document_sections.content: For women with pre-existing or gestational diabetes, follow the NICE guidance on diabetes in pregnancy. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 1.2 Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
document_sections.content: Interpret proteinuria alongside a complete clinical assessment of symptoms, signs and other findings relevant to pre-eclampsia. In secondary care, use an automated reagent-strip reader for initial dipstick screening; a result of 1+ or more should be quantified with an albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio. Do not use the first morning urine void for quantification, and do not routinely collect urine over 24 hours. For protein:creatinine ratio, the threshold for significant proteinuria is 30 mg/mmol; if the result is 30 mg/mmol or above but diagnosis remains uncertain, consider a fresh sample and another clinical assessment. When albumin:creatinine ratio is used instead to diagnose pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension, apply a threshold of 8 mg/mmol and consider repeat testing on a new sample with clinical review if a result of 8 mg/mmol or above leaves diagnostic uncertainty. [2019]

document_sections.heading: Pre-pregnancy advice
document_sections.content: Offer women with chronic hypertension referral to a specialist in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy to discuss treatment benefits and risks. Explain to women taking angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) that exposure during pregnancy increases the risk of congenital abnormalities; women planning pregnancy should discuss another antihypertensive, including when these medicines are being used for another condition such as renal disease. If pregnancy occurs, stop ACE inhibitors or ARBs, preferably within 2 working days of notification, and offer an alternative. Explain that thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics may increase the risk of congenital abnormalities and neonatal complications, and advise discussion of another treatment before pregnancy. For antihypertensives outside these groups, explain that the limited available evidence has not shown increased congenital malformation risk. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] The MHRA's 2014 warning advises avoiding ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists when pregnancy is planned unless essential, with discussion of benefits and risks if they are necessary.

document_sections.heading: Treatment of chronic hypertension
document_sections.content: Offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension advice on weight management, exercise, healthy eating and reducing dietary salt, consistent with NICE guidance for hypertension in adults. Continue an existing pregnancy-safe antihypertensive or change to a suitable alternative unless sustained systolic pressure is less than 110 mmHg, sustained diastolic pressure is less than 70 mmHg, or symptomatic hypotension occurs. Offer treatment to an untreated woman when sustained systolic pressure is 140 mmHg or higher or sustained diastolic pressure is 90 mmHg or higher; aim for 135/85 mmHg with medicines. Consider labetalol, then nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, then methyldopa if both are unsuitable; consider existing treatment, adverse effects, fetal and other risks, and preference. Offer aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg once daily from 12 weeks. If pre-eclampsia is suspected, offer PLGF-based testing between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days to help rule it out. [2019; 2019, amended 2023] At publication in June 2019, some nifedipine brands were manufacturer-contraindicated in pregnancy, so check the preparation's product information. Aspirin lacked UK authorisation for this indication despite common use and, in England, requires a prescription rather than pharmacy sale for prevention of pre-eclampsia.

document_sections.heading: Antenatal appointments
document_sections.content: Arrange extra appointments according to maternal and fetal needs in chronic hypertension. This may mean weekly visits when control is poor or visits every 2 to 4 weeks when control is good. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Timing of birth
document_sections.content: For chronic hypertension with pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg, do not offer planned early birth before 37 weeks without another medical indication. After 37 weeks at pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg, the woman and senior obstetrician should agree when birth is appropriate and which maternal or fetal indications apply. If early birth is needed, offer antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate when indicated, following NICE guidance on preterm labour and birth. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] For gestational hypertension with pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg, likewise do not offer planned early birth before 37 weeks without another medical reason; after 37 weeks, agree timing and indications with the woman and senior obstetrician. When early birth is necessary, offer antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate if indicated. [2010, amended 2019] In pre-eclampsia, document maternal and fetal thresholds for birth before 37 weeks. Possible triggers include pressure uncontrolled despite 3 or more appropriately dosed antihypertensive classes, maternal pulse oximetry less than 90%, worsening liver or kidney function, haemolysis or platelet count, persistent serious neurological features or eclampsia, placental abruption, reversed umbilical artery end-diastolic flow, a nonreassuring cardiotocograph, or stillbirth; other features may also matter. Involve a senior obstetrician, discuss planned birth with anaesthesia, and involve neonatology when neonatal complications are expected. For planned early birth with preterm pre-eclampsia, offer intravenous magnesium sulfate and antenatal corticosteroids if indicated. The gestational-age decisions are presented in table 3. [2010, amended 2019; 2019] Pulse oximeters can give values that are too low or too high, especially near a threshold; overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin.

document_sections.heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment
document_sections.content: After birth in chronic hypertension, check pressure daily for the first 2 days, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and as clinically indicated after a medication change. Aim for pressure lower than 140/90 mmHg, continue treatment if required, and offer a GP or specialist medication review 2 weeks after birth. Stop methyldopa used for chronic hypertension within 2 days after birth and substitute another antihypertensive. Offer a further medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] In gestational hypertension, use the same initial blood-pressure measurement schedule. Continue medicines if necessary, explain that postnatal treatment usually lasts about as long as antenatal treatment but can last longer, and reduce treatment if pressure falls below 130/80 mmHg. Stop methyldopa within 2 days after birth and substitute another treatment if needed; start medication at 150/100 mmHg or higher in women who received no antenatal antihypertensive. A transfer plan must specify the follow-up provider and any medical review, measurement frequency, thresholds to reduce or stop medication, and indications for primary-care assessment. Offer women still receiving medication a review 2 weeks after transfer, and all women a review 6 to 8 weeks after birth. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: A professional trained in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders should conduct a full assessment in secondary care. Account for nulliparity, age 40 years or older, an inter-pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, family history of pre-eclampsia, multi-fetal pregnancy, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more, gestational age at presentation, prior pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension, and existing vascular or kidney disease when deciding on additional assessment and follow-up. Offer the investigations and treatment in table 1. Offer PLGF-based testing between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days when pre-eclampsia is suspected, to help rule it out. Consider labetalol, followed by nifedipine if unsuitable and methyldopa if either is unsuitable, taking account of adverse effects, fetal and other risks, and preferences. Do not offer hospital bed rest as treatment. [2010; 2010, amended 2019; 2019; 2019, amended 2023] In June 2019, some nifedipine brands were manufacturer-contraindicated during pregnancy; consult information for the specific product.

document_sections.heading: Assessing pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: A professional trained in pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders should assess pre-eclampsia. Perform a complete clinical assessment at every antenatal visit and offer admission for observation or intervention if maternal or fetal wellbeing raises concern. Examples include sustained systolic pressure of 160 mmHg or higher; a new, persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more; alanine transaminase over 70 IU/litre or twice the upper limit of normal; platelets under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe features; suspected fetal compromise; or other concerning clinical findings. Consider fullPIERS or PREP-S alongside assessment to inform care location, possible in utero transfer and intervention thresholds. fullPIERS may be used at any pregnancy stage, whereas PREP-S is intended only up to 34 weeks; neither predicts infant outcomes. [2010, amended 2019; 2019]

document_sections.heading: Treatment of pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: Offer the tests and management specified in table 2. Offer labetalol for hypertension associated with pre-eclampsia; if unsuitable, offer nifedipine, and if both are unsuitable, offer methyldopa. Select treatment according to previous medicines, adverse effects, fetal and other risks, and the woman's preference. [2019; 2010, amended 2019] Some nifedipine brands carried a manufacturer contraindication during pregnancy at publication in June 2019; consult the product-specific information.

document_sections.heading: Blood pressure
document_sections.content: After birth in pre-eclampsia without antihypertensive treatment, check pressure at least 4 times a day in hospital, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and on alternate days until normal if abnormal on days 3 to 5. Begin treatment if pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher, and ask about severe headache and epigastric pain whenever pressure is measured. If antihypertensives were used, measure pressure at least 4 times a day in hospital and every 1 to 2 days for up to 2 weeks following transfer to community care, until treatment has ended and hypertension has resolved. Continue treatment after birth; consider reducing it below 140/90 mmHg and reduce it below 130/80 mmHg. Stop methyldopa within 2 days after birth and use an alternative if needed. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] Offer community transfer only when symptoms of pre-eclampsia are absent, pressure with or without treatment is 150/100 mmHg or less, and blood results are stable or improving. Specify follow-up responsibility, pressure-check frequency, treatment-reduction or cessation thresholds, primary-care referral indications and symptom self-monitoring in the transfer plan. Offer a medical review 2 weeks after transfer for women still taking antihypertensives, and a review 6 to 8 weeks after birth for all women who had pre-eclampsia. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Haematological and biochemical monitoring
document_sections.content: For pre-eclampsia with mild or moderate hypertension, or after leaving critical care, measure platelets, transaminases and serum creatinine 48 to 72 hours after birth or step-down; do not repeat normal results at that point. Repeat results outside reference ranges when clinically indicated until they normalise. Perform a urinary reagent-strip test 6 to 8 weeks after birth. If proteinuria remains 1+ or more then, offer another GP or specialist review at 3 months to assess kidney function; consider specialist kidney assessment if function is abnormal at 3 months. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Fetal monitoring in chronic hypertension
document_sections.content: Assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery doppler velocimetry by ultrasound at 28 weeks, 32 weeks and 36 weeks. Use cardiotocography only when clinically indicated. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Fetal monitoring in gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: At diagnosis, assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery doppler velocimetry by ultrasound; if normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks when clinically indicated. Perform cardiotocography only when clinically indicated. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: Perform cardiotocography at diagnosis. If conservative management is planned, also assess fetal growth, amniotic fluid volume and umbilical artery doppler velocimetry at diagnosis. If all findings are normal, do not routinely repeat cardiotocography without a clinical indication; repeat it for changed fetal movement, vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain or deteriorating maternal condition. Repeat the ultrasound assessment of growth and fluid volume or umbilical artery doppler velocimetry every 2 weeks, with later monitoring guided by results. Document future fetal monitoring, fetal indications for birth, whether and when to give antenatal corticosteroids, and plans to consult neonatal paediatricians and obstetric anaesthetists. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Women who need additional fetal monitoring
document_sections.content: For women with previous severe pre-eclampsia, pre-eclampsia leading to birth before 34 weeks, pre-eclampsia with infant birth weight below the 10th centile, intrauterine death or placental abruption, begin ultrasound assessment of fetal growth, amniotic fluid and umbilical artery doppler velocimetry between 28 and 30 weeks, or at least 2 weeks before an earlier previous gestational age of onset, and repeat 4 weeks later. Use cardiotocography only when clinically indicated. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: 1.7 Intrapartum care
document_sections.content: Provide care for hypertensive disorders according to NICE intrapartum guidance unless this guideline gives a recommendation on the same subject. Hypertension in labour should receive appropriate intrapartum care whether treated or untreated, not determined solely by the pressure during labour. For chronic hypertension, also follow NICE intrapartum guidance concerning pre-existing medical conditions or obstetric complications. [2010, amended 2019; 2019]

document_sections.heading: Blood pressure
document_sections.content: In labour, check blood pressure hourly in women with hypertension and every 15 to 30 minutes in severe hypertension until it is less than 160/110 mmHg. Continue antenatal antihypertensive medication during labour. [2010; 2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Haematological and biochemical monitoring
document_sections.content: Use the antenatal criteria to decide whether blood tests are needed during labour in women with hypertension, including when regional analgesia is under consideration. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Care during epidural analgesia
document_sections.content: Do not preload women with severe pre-eclampsia with intravenous fluid before low-dose epidural or combined spinal epidural analgesia. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Management of second stage of labour
document_sections.content: Do not routinely shorten the second stage when hypertension is controlled. Consider operative or assisted birth during the second stage for severe hypertension unresponsive to initial treatment. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Anticonvulsants
document_sections.content: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate in critical care to a woman with severe hypertension or severe pre-eclampsia who has had an eclamptic fit. Consider it for severe pre-eclampsia in critical care when birth is planned within 24 hours. Consider treatment when 1 or more severe features occur: persistent or recurring severe headache, visual scotomata, nausea or vomiting, epigastric pain, oliguria with severe hypertension, or progressive worsening of creatinine, liver transaminases or platelet count. Use the Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen: 4 g intravenously over 5 to 15 minutes, followed by 1 g/hour for 24 hours; after a fit, continue infusion for 24 hours after the last fit. Treat recurrent fits with another 2 g to 4 g intravenously over 5 to 15 minutes. Do not substitute diazepam, phenytoin or another anticonvulsant for magnesium sulfate in eclampsia. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] The MHRA warns of neonatal skeletal adverse effects after prolonged or repeated maternal magnesium sulfate. Maternal use longer than 5 to 7 days has been associated with neonatal skeletal effects, hypocalcaemia and hypermagnesemia; consider checking neonatal calcium, magnesium and skeletal effects after prolonged or repeated use.

document_sections.heading: Antihypertensives
document_sections.content: Immediately treat severe hypertension in critical care during pregnancy or after birth with oral or intravenous labetalol, oral nifedipine, or intravenous hydralazine. Check for pressure reduction and adverse maternal or infant effects, and adjust treatment according to response. Consider up to 500 ml of crystalloid before or with the first antenatal intravenous hydralazine dose. [2010; 2010, amended 2019] At publication in June 2019, manufacturer information specifically contraindicated some nifedipine brands in pregnancy; check the individual preparation.

document_sections.heading: Corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation
document_sections.content: If birth within 7 days is considered likely for a woman with pre-eclampsia, offer a course of antenatal corticosteroids in accordance with NICE guidance on preterm labour and birth. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Corticosteroids to manage HELLP syndrome
document_sections.content: Do not treat HELLP syndrome with dexamethasone or betamethasone. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Fluid balance and volume expansion
document_sections.content: Do not expand circulating volume in severe pre-eclampsia unless antenatal antihypertensive treatment is hydralazine. Limit maintenance fluid to 80 ml/hour unless additional fluid loss, such as haemorrhage, is ongoing. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Caesarean section versus induction of labour
document_sections.content: For severe hypertension, severe pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, choose the mode of birth according to clinical circumstances and the woman's preference. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Referral to critical care
document_sections.content: Refer women with severe hypertension or severe pre-eclampsia to an appropriate critical-care level using the clinical criteria shown in table 4. [2010]

document_sections.heading: 1.9 Antihypertensive treatment during the postnatal period, including during breastfeeding
document_sections.content: Explain that antihypertensive treatment can be adapted for breastfeeding and does not itself prevent it. Medicines can enter milk, but most antihypertensives result in very low milk concentrations and infant exposure unlikely to have clinical effects. Manufacturer disclaimers often reflect a lack of testing in pregnant or breastfeeding women rather than specific evidence of harm; agree treatment with the woman according to her preferences. Consider checking blood pressure in symptomatic infants, particularly preterm infants, during the first few weeks, and advise mothers after discharge to watch for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold extremities or poor feeding. [2019] Offer enalapril after birth with appropriate maternal kidney-function and serum-potassium monitoring. For women of black African or Caribbean family origin, consider nifedipine or amlodipine if amlodipine previously controlled their pressure successfully. If a single drug is insufficient, consider nifedipine or amlodipine with enalapril; if that combination fails or is not tolerated, consider adding atenolol or labetalol or replacing 1 medicine with either. Prefer once-daily medicines where possible. Where possible, avoid diuretics and angiotensin receptor blockers during breastfeeding or milk expression. For women neither breastfeeding nor planning to do so, use NICE guidance on hypertension in adults. [2010, amended 2019; 2019] An MHRA clarification in 2014 states that ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor antagonists are generally not recommended in breastfeeding but are not absolutely contraindicated if essential for the mother. For mothers feeding older infants, captopril, enalapril or quinapril may be considered if an ACE inhibitor is necessary, with careful infant follow-up for hypotension. As noted at publication in June 2019, some nifedipine brands had a manufacturer pregnancy contraindication.

document_sections.heading: Risk of recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
document_sections.content: Tell women with a hypertensive pregnancy disorder that recurrence of a hypertensive disorder in a later pregnancy is approximately 1 in 5. Table 5 presents recurrence estimates according to the earlier disorder and the disorder in the later pregnancy. [2019]

document_sections.heading: Long-term risk of cardiovascular disease
document_sections.content: Explain that a hypertensive disorder during pregnancy is associated with greater risk of later hypertension and cardiovascular disease; table 6 summarises the relative-risk estimates by disorder and outcome. These estimates combine risk ratios, odds ratios and hazard ratios against women without a hypertensive pregnancy disorder; absolute risks are not given because follow-up varies from 1 to 40 years postpartum. Advise discussion with a GP or specialist about lowering cardiovascular and hypertensive-disorder risk, including avoiding smoking and maintaining a healthy lifestyle and weight. Consider counselling before another pregnancy after pre-eclampsia or hypertension associated with birth before 34 weeks, to discuss recurrence risks and ways to lower them. [2019]

document_sections.heading: Body mass index and recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
document_sections.content: Advise women with previous pre-eclampsia to reach and maintain a healthy BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 kg/m2 before another pregnancy. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Inter-pregnancy interval and recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
document_sections.content: Explain after pre-eclampsia that recurrence becomes more likely when the interval between pregnancies exceeds 10 years. [2010, amended 2019]

document_sections.heading: Long-term risk of end-stage kidney disease
document_sections.content: For women with prior pre-eclampsia who have neither proteinuria nor hypertension at the review 6 to 8 weeks after birth, explain that the relative risk of end-stage kidney disease is higher but its absolute risk is low, so no additional follow-up is required. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Thrombophilia and the risk of pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: Do not routinely screen for thrombophilia after pre-eclampsia. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Chronic hypertension
document_sections.content: This means hypertension present at the booking visit or before 20 weeks, or already treated with an antihypertensive when the woman is referred to maternity services. Its cause may be primary or secondary.

document_sections.heading: Eclampsia
document_sections.content: This is a convulsive condition occurring in association with pre-eclampsia.

document_sections.heading: Gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: This is newly presenting hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy without significant proteinuria.

document_sections.heading: HELLP syndrome
document_sections.content: The term denotes haemolysis, increased liver enzymes and a low platelet count.

document_sections.heading: Hypertension
document_sections.content: The definition is systolic blood pressure of 140 mmHg or higher or diastolic pressure of 90 mmHg or higher. [2019]

document_sections.heading: Multi-fetal pregnancy
document_sections.content: This means a pregnancy involving more than 1 baby, such as twins or triplets.

document_sections.heading: Pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: The definition requires new hypertension after 20 weeks, with systolic pressure over 140 mmHg or diastolic pressure over 90 mmHg, together with 1 or more newly occurring features: proteinuria, maternal organ dysfunction or uteroplacental dysfunction. Proteinuria may be a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 30 mg/mmol or more, albumin:creatinine ratio of 8 mg/mmol or more, or at least 1 g/litre [2+] on dipstick testing. Organ dysfunction includes creatinine 90 micromol/litre or more, 1.02 mg/100 ml or more; alanine aminotransferase or aspartate aminotransferase over 40 IU/litre, with or without right upper-quadrant or epigastric pain; eclampsia, altered mental status, blindness, stroke, clonus, severe headache or persistent visual scotomata; or platelets below 150,000/microlitre, disseminated intravascular coagulation or haemolysis. Uteroplacental dysfunction includes restricted fetal growth, abnormal umbilical artery doppler waveforms or stillbirth.

document_sections.heading: Severe hypertension
document_sections.content: This is blood pressure over 160 mmHg systolic or over 110 mmHg diastolic.

document_sections.heading: Severe pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: This is pre-eclampsia with severe hypertension that does not respond to treatment or occurs with persistent or recurring severe headache, visual scotomata, nausea or vomiting, epigastric pain, oliguria and severe hypertension, progressive worsening of creatinine or liver transaminases or falling platelets, failure of fetal growth, or abnormal doppler findings.

document_sections.heading: 1 Management of chronic hypertension in pregnancy
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question asks for head-to-head evidence on the effectiveness and safety of antihypertensive medicines in improving maternal and perinatal outcomes among pregnant women needing treatment for chronic hypertension. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 2 Management of hypertension in pregnancy
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question concerns adverse neonatal outcomes associated with maternal beta blockers or mixed alpha-beta blockers when hypertension requires treatment during pregnancy. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 3 Management of pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question asks which women with pre-eclampsia and which babies obtain better outcomes with inpatient management. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 4 Antihypertensive treatment during the postnatal period
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question asks how effective and safe antihypertensive medicines are at achieving adequate control after birth, including during breastfeeding. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 5 Fetal monitoring
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question asks which fetal-monitoring strategy best detects infants who are small for gestational age when pregnancy is affected by hypertension. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 6 Advice and follow-up at transfer to community care
document_sections.content: The 2019 research question asks which interventions following hypertension in pregnancy reduce recurrence of a hypertensive pregnancy disorder or later cardiovascular disease. [2019]

document_sections.heading: 7 Haematological and biochemical monitoring in women with gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: The 2010 research question concerns the value of haematological and biochemical assessment at gestational-hypertension diagnosis and during subsequent surveillance. [2010]

document_sections.heading: Assessment of proteinuria
document_sections.content: The committee cautioned against diagnosing pre-eclampsia from proteinuria alone: hypertension severity and other clinical findings also matter. It favoured automated rather than visual dipstick assessment in secondary care because visual assessment has a higher error rate. Evidence showed high sensitivity and specificity for both protein:creatinine ratio at 30 mg/mmol and albumin:creatinine ratio at 8 mg/mmol; using both together added no diagnostic benefit. Some evidence indicated poorer accuracy with a first morning sample. Spot ratios were preferred to 24-hour collection because the latter is burdensome and can delay diagnosis, although rare circumstances such as renal complications may justify collection over 24 hours. Variation in daily protein excretion supports repeat testing when a protein:creatinine ratio above 30 mg/mmol leaves uncertainty. A single study supported albumin:creatinine ratio at 8 mg/mmol, with further evidence from a large UK study for severe pre-eclampsia; this pregnancy threshold differs from the non-pregnant microalbuminuria threshold. Repeat albumin:creatinine ratio may prevent overdiagnosis after one elevated result. Evidence did not establish when either ratio should be repeated. The committee anticipated that fuller assessment might increase surveillance while reducing missed disease, automated readers might require investment but improve screening, and spot samples might speed diagnosis and ease collection. Repeat testing might add a small cost but reduce false positives and unnecessary intensive follow-up or admission.

document_sections.heading: Treatment of chronic hypertension
document_sections.content: The committee aligned lifestyle advice with adult-hypertension guidance. Evidence on when to start treatment was very limited, so thresholds drew on the Control of Hypertension in Pregnancy Study (CHIPS) and adult guidance; the large CHIPS trial informed the blood-pressure target. Evidence comparing medicines showed limited benefits and harms without enough certainty to prefer one on that basis. Prior guideline use and longstanding pregnancy experience supported labetalol, nifedipine and methyldopa; labetalol was suggested first because it is licensed for pregnancy, nifedipine next, and methyldopa third because it may cause more adverse effects and be the least effective of the 3. Evidence for aspirin reducing preterm birth and neonatal-unit admission was very limited. Studies used 50 mg to 150 mg daily, while common UK practice was 75 mg to 150 mg, supporting the recommended range. The committee cross-referenced diabetes guidance because chronic hypertension is linked with pre-existing and gestational diabetes, and PLGF guidance because testing may apply in chronic hypertension. A lack of comparative drug-outcome evidence and concerns about possible neonatal effects of beta blockers motivated research questions. The target was expected to make care more consistent; treatment initiation and aspirin were already standard care, so major practice change was not expected.

document_sections.heading: Monitoring and treatment of gestational hypertension
document_sections.content: The committee revised the gestational-hypertension management table. Evidence on treatment-start thresholds was very limited, so it used values from CHIPS; evidence from the large CHIPS trial informed the target pressure. It added a reference to PLGF-based testing and cross-referenced diabetes guidance because gestational hypertension is linked to pre-existing and gestational diabetes. No evidence was available on fetal monitoring in gestational hypertension, prompting a research question about detecting infants small for gestational age. The recommendations reflected existing practice in many units but might harmonise targets across the NHS.

document_sections.heading: Assessment of women with pre-eclampsia
document_sections.content: Clinical expertise led the committee to favour assessment at every antenatal appointment and admission when maternal or infant wellbeing is in doubt, including but not limited to severe hypertension or other high-risk features. Some evidence supported fullPIERS and PREP-S for identifying different maternal risks. fullPIERS had more extensive validation across varied care settings; PREP-S was developed in a UK population and validated using comparable multinational data, but further validation was considered unlikely because of cost. Both may supplement, not replace, clinical assessment when choosing care setting or intervention. Neither predicts infant outcomes. Their use might make admission decisions more consistent, increasing admissions in some centres and decreasing them in others.

document_sections.heading: Monitoring and treatment of pre-eclampsia and timing of birth
document_sections.content: The committee revised the management table. Limited evidence on place of care supported admission when maternal or fetal wellbeing raises concern or fullPIERS or PREP-S predicts high complication risk. There was no direct evidence on treatment-start thresholds or target pressure for pre-eclampsia, so the committee drew on adult-hypertension guidance and CHIPS values from women with chronic or gestational hypertension. Evidence comparing medicines was too limited to establish a preferred drug by benefit and harm; the choices retained from the previous guideline account for previous treatment, adverse effects and preference. labetalol was suggested first because it is licensed for pregnancy, nifedipine next and methyldopa third, which may have more adverse effects and be least effective of the 3. Limited evidence comparing early planned birth with expectant management supported decisions based on maternal and fetal risk from continuing pregnancy. HYPITAT-II data also supported surveillance until 37 weeks unless a specific concern justified earlier birth. Uncertainty about the best place of care prompted a research recommendation. The committee expected little overall change in best clinical practice, although admissions could rise or fall locally as practice becomes more consistent.

document_sections.heading: Antihypertensive treatment during the postnatal period, including during breastfeeding
document_sections.content: Evidence on postnatal antihypertensive effectiveness and safety was very limited. The committee adapted adult-hypertension guidance for possible infant exposure: an ACE inhibitor was favoured initially except for women of African or Caribbean family origin, for whom a calcium-channel blocker was favoured. Because angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics are not recommended while breastfeeding, the committee favoured beta-blockers as the next antihypertensive option. It preferred once-daily treatment when possible: enalapril rather than captopril, which is taken 3 times daily, and atenolol as an alternative to labetalol, which is taken 2 to 4 times daily. Experience informed advice about breastfeeding and infant monitoring. The limited evidence prompted revision of a research question from 2010. Recommendations might reduce marked variation in postnatal practice and increase atenolol use instead of labetalol.

document_sections.heading: Risk of recurrence of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and long-term cardiovascular disease
document_sections.content: Long-term follow-up studies found more cardiovascular disease later in life and more hypertensive disorders in subsequent pregnancies after an affected pregnancy than among women without such a history. The committee found no evidence establishing interventions that lower either recurrence or future cardiovascular risk, prompting a research recommendation. Providing advice about future risks and relevant lifestyle or clinical support might add work in some settings.

document_sections.heading: Context
document_sections.content: Hypertensive disorders affect around 8% to 10% of pregnant women and can cause major maternal and infant complications. Hypertension may predate pregnancy or arise in the first 20 weeks as chronic hypertension, develop later as gestational hypertension, or occur with multi-organ features as pre-eclampsia. Overall prevalence appears fairly stable, but maternal mortality from hypertensive causes has fallen substantially: less than 1 woman in every million who gives birth now dies from pre-eclampsia. The document reports consensus that the 2010 NICE guideline and findings from the confidential enquiry into maternal deaths contributed importantly to this decline. Nonetheless, maternal illness, stillbirth, neonatal death and perinatal illness remain substantial, and later cardiovascular risk is higher. Variation in care contributes to unequal outcomes. The update addressed new evidence on chronic and gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, breastfeeding, and advice and follow-up after transfer to community care. It did not evaluate pre-eclampsia screening strategies or alternative ways to group all pregnancy-related hypertension for treatment. It clarified the pre-eclampsia definition to better align with the International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy (ISSHP). The 2019 guideline aims to update evidence-based care while identifying research gaps and reducing unnecessary variation.

document_sections.heading: Update information
document_sections.content: In April 2023, the recommended timing of PLGF-based testing in recommendations 1.3.12 and 1.4.4 was aligned with related diagnostic guidance. In June 2019, evidence was reviewed for proteinuria assessment, treatment of chronic and gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia, breastfeeding, and advice at discharge; recommendations based on that review are marked [2019]. Other amendments clarified aspirin dosage, pre-eclampsia and planned early birth advice, physical activity, risks of ACE inhibitors and thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics, postnatal treatment including methyldopa, fetal testing schedules, care plans, anticonvulsants, and angiotensin-receptor blockers during breastfeeding; these are marked [2010, amended 2019]. Recommendations marked [2010] last underwent evidence review in 2010. In October 2022, information was added on reduced pulse-oximetry reliability in people with dark skin. In August 2022, 'nulliparity' replaced 'first pregnancy' in recommendation 1.1.3.

recommendations.statement: Tell pregnant women to seek immediate professional assessment if they develop possible symptoms of pre-eclampsia, including a severe headache, visual disturbance, severe pain beneath the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

Advise pregnant women with any high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia to take 75 mg to 150 mg of aspirin daily from 12 weeks until birth. High-risk factors are hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, and chronic hypertension.
recommendations.context: Aspirin for this indication must be prescribed.

recommendations.statement: Advise pregnant women with more than 1 moderate-risk factor for pre-eclampsia to take 75 mg to 150 mg of aspirin daily from 12 weeks until birth. Moderate-risk factors are nulliparity, age 40 years or older, a pregnancy interval of more than 10 years, BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more at the first visit, a family history of pre-eclampsia, and multi-fetal pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Aspirin for this indication must be prescribed.

recommendations.statement: Do not use nitric oxide donors, progesterone, diuretics or low molecular weight heparin to prevent hypertensive disorders during pregnancy.
Do not recommend magnesium, folic acid, antioxidants (vitamins C and E), fish oils or algal oils, or garlic solely to prevent hypertensive disorders during pregnancy.
Do not advise restricting salt during pregnancy solely to prevent gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia.
Give women with chronic hypertension or a risk of hypertensive disorders during pregnancy the same guidance on rest, exercise and work as healthy pregnant women.
recommendations.context: Refer to the NICE guideline on antenatal care.

recommendations.statement: For women with pre-existing diabetes or gestational diabetes, follow the NICE guideline on diabetes in pregnancy.
Interpret proteinuria results in pregnant women alongside a complete clinical evaluation of symptoms, signs and other investigations relevant to pre-eclampsia.
recommendations.rationale: A proteinuria result alone may lead to an inappropriate diagnosis because pre-eclampsia has manifestations beyond proteinuria.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: In secondary care, screen pregnant women for proteinuria using a reagent-strip device that reads results automatically.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered visual interpretation more prone to error.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: If a pregnant woman's dipstick screen is positive at 1+ or more, quantify proteinuria using an albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio.
recommendations.rationale: Both ratios showed high diagnostic sensitivity and specificity at the selected thresholds.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: Do not use the first morning urine void to quantify proteinuria in pregnant women.
recommendations.rationale: Some evidence suggested that this sample may reduce diagnostic accuracy.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: Do not routinely quantify proteinuria in pregnant women by collecting urine over 24 hours.
recommendations.rationale: Spot urine ratios have high diagnostic accuracy; a 24-hour collection is burdensome and can delay identification, although it may occasionally be more appropriate, such as with renal complications.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: When quantifying proteinuria with the protein:creatinine ratio, use 30 mg/mmol as the threshold for significant proteinuria. If the result is 30 mg/mmol or above but the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia remains uncertain, consider testing a new sample and reviewing the woman clinically.
recommendations.rationale: Protein excretion varies within and between days, so an isolated raised result may otherwise lead to overdiagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: When using the albumin:creatinine ratio instead of the protein:creatinine ratio to diagnose pre-eclampsia in a pregnant woman with hypertension, use 8 mg/mmol as the diagnostic threshold. If the result is 8 mg/mmol or above and diagnostic uncertainty persists, consider repeating the test on a new sample together with clinical review.
recommendations.rationale: The selected threshold had supporting diagnostic evidence, while reliance on a single raised result could lead to overdiagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment of proteinuria in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

recommendations.statement: Offer women with chronic hypertension a referral to a specialist in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy to discuss treatment benefits and risks.
recommendations.context: Pre-pregnancy advice.

recommendations.statement: Tell women taking angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) that use during pregnancy increases the risk of congenital abnormalities. If they plan pregnancy, advise discussion of another antihypertensive with the professional managing their hypertension; if they take these medicines for another condition, such as renal disease, advise discussion of alternative treatment with the professional managing that condition.
recommendations.context: Pre-pregnancy advice.

recommendations.statement: If a woman taking ACE inhibitors or ARBs becomes pregnant, stop that antihypertensive treatment, preferably within 2 working days of notification of pregnancy, and offer an alternative.

Tell women taking thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics that use during pregnancy may increase the risk of congenital abnormalities and neonatal complications. If they are planning pregnancy, advise them to discuss alternative antihypertensive treatment with the professional managing their hypertension.

Tell women taking antihypertensives other than ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide or thiazide-like diuretics that the limited available evidence has not shown an increased risk of congenital malformation with those treatments.
Offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension guidance on weight management, exercise, healthy eating and reducing dietary salt, consistent with the NICE guideline on hypertension in adults.

Continue an existing antihypertensive if it is safe in pregnancy, or change to another treatment, unless sustained systolic blood pressure is less than 110 mmHg, sustained diastolic blood pressure is less than 70 mmHg, or the woman has symptomatic hypotension.
recommendations.context: Pregnant women with chronic hypertension.

recommendations.statement: Offer antihypertensive medication to a pregnant woman with chronic hypertension who is not already receiving it when sustained systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg or higher or sustained diastolic blood pressure is 90 mmHg or higher.
When treating hypertension in pregnancy with medication, aim for blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg.

Consider labetalol for chronic hypertension in pregnancy; consider nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, or methyldopa if both are unsuitable. Choose in light of prior treatment, adverse-effect profiles, risks including fetal effects, and the woman's preference.
recommendations.context: At publication, some nifedipine brands were specifically contraindicated during pregnancy in their manufacturers' product information.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence comparing antihypertensives was insufficient to establish one as superior; the committee identified these as preferred options based partly on previous guideline use.

recommendations.statement: Offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg once daily from 12 weeks.
recommendations.context: Aspirin for prevention of pre-eclampsia in pregnancy must be prescribed.
recommendations.rationale: Very limited evidence suggested benefits for preterm birth and neonatal unit admission; the recommended dose range also reflected UK practice.

recommendations.statement: Offer placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia when a woman with chronic hypertension is suspected of developing it between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
recommendations.context: See the NICE diagnostics guidance on PLGF-based testing for suspected preterm pre-eclampsia.

recommendations.statement: Arrange extra antenatal visits for women with chronic hypertension according to maternal and fetal needs; this may mean weekly visits when hypertension is poorly controlled or visits every 2 to 4 weeks when it is well controlled.

Do not offer planned early birth before 37 weeks to a woman with chronic hypertension and blood pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg, regardless of antihypertensive treatment, unless another medical indication exists.

After 37 weeks, agree the timing of birth and maternal and fetal indications for birth between the woman and a senior obstetrician when chronic hypertension is accompanied by blood pressure lower than 160/ 110 mmHg, whether or not she receives antihypertensives.
If planned early birth is needed, offer a course of antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate if indicated, consistent with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth.
recommendations.context: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy.

recommendations.statement: After birth, measure blood pressure in women with chronic hypertension daily for the first 2 days, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and as clinically indicated if postnatal antihypertensive treatment changes.

After birth in women with chronic hypertension, aim to maintain blood pressure lower than 140/90 mmHg, continue antihypertensives if needed, and offer review of treatment with a GP or specialist 2 weeks after birth.
If methyldopa was used for chronic hypertension during pregnancy, stop it within 2 days after birth and change to another antihypertensive.
Offer women with chronic hypertension a medical review with their GP or specialist, as appropriate, 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
Arrange a comprehensive assessment in secondary care for women with gestational hypertension, performed by a professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: In gestational hypertension, account for factors requiring additional assessment and follow-up: nulliparity; age 40 years or older; a pregnancy interval of more than 10 years; family history of pre-eclampsia; multi-fetal pregnancy; BMI of 35 kg/m2 or more; gestational age at presentation; previous pre-eclampsia or gestational hypertension; and pre-existing vascular or kidney disease.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Provide the assessment and treatment specified for gestational hypertension: without severe hypertension, do not routinely admit; offer medication if BP remains above 140/90 mmHg, target 135/85 mmHg or less, measure BP and test urine protein once or twice a week, and check full blood count, liver and renal function at presentation and weekly. With severe hypertension, admit and offer medication to all women; if BP falls below 160/ 110 mmHg, manage as hypertension. Target 135/85 mmHg or less; measure BP every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110 mmHg and test urine protein daily during admission. Perform the same blood tests at presentation and weekly. In either group, perform PLGF-based testing on 1 occasion if pre-eclampsia is suspected and assess the fetus as specified in the table.
recommendations.context: Fetal assessment comprises auscultation at every antenatal appointment and ultrasound at diagnosis. If normal, repeat ultrasound every 2 to 4 weeks when clinically indicated without severe hypertension, or every 2 weeks if severe hypertension persists. Perform CTG only if clinically indicated without severe hypertension; with severe hypertension, perform it at diagnosis and subsequently only if indicated.
recommendations.rationale: The committee updated its management table using available evidence on blood pressure targets and, because initiation-threshold evidence was very limited, values from CHIPS.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Offer placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia when suspected pre-eclampsia presents, for example alongside gestational hypertension, between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy.
recommendations.context: See the NICE diagnostics guidance on PLGF-based testing for suspected preterm pre-eclampsia.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Consider labetalol for gestational hypertension; consider nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, and methyldopa if labetalol or nifedipine is unsuitable. Base the choice on adverse-effect profiles, risks including fetal effects, and the woman's preferences.
recommendations.context: At publication, some nifedipine brands were specifically contraindicated during pregnancy in their manufacturers' product information.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Do not offer hospital bed rest as treatment for gestational hypertension.
recommendations.source_heading: Assessment and treatment of gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Do not offer planned early birth before 37 weeks for gestational hypertension with blood pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg unless there is another medical indication.

After 37 weeks, a woman with gestational hypertension and blood pressure lower than 160/110 mmHg should agree the timing of birth and maternal and fetal indications for birth with a senior obstetrician.
When planned early birth is necessary, offer a course of antenatal corticosteroids and magnesium sulfate if indicated, in accordance with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth.
recommendations.context: Gestational hypertension in pregnancy.

recommendations.statement: After birth in women with gestational hypertension, measure blood pressure daily for the first 2 days, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and whenever clinically indicated following a change in antihypertensive treatment.

After birth in women with gestational hypertension, continue antihypertensives when needed, explain that postnatal treatment usually lasts about as long as antenatal treatment but may last longer, and reduce treatment if blood pressure falls below 130/ 80 mmHg.
If methyldopa was taken for gestational hypertension, stop it within 2 days after birth and change treatment if needed.
Start antihypertensive treatment after birth if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher in a woman with gestational hypertension who did not receive antihypertensives.

For transfer to community care after gestational hypertension, document who will provide follow-up and any needed medical review, the frequency of blood pressure checks, thresholds for reducing or stopping treatment, and reasons to refer for blood pressure review in primary care.
Offer a GP or specialist review 2 weeks after transfer to community care to women who have had gestational hypertension and remain on antihypertensives.
Offer every woman who has had gestational hypertension a GP or specialist medical review 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
Have a professional trained in managing hypertensive disorders of pregnancy assess women with pre-eclampsia.

Perform a full clinical assessment at every antenatal visit for women with pre-eclampsia. Offer admission for surveillance and required interventions if maternal or fetal wellbeing is concerning, including sustained systolic BP of 160 mmHg or higher; a new persistent rise in creatinine to 90 micromol/litre or more, 1 mg/100 ml or more, or alanine transaminase over 70 IU/litre or twice the upper normal limit; platelets under 150,000/microlitre; impending eclampsia or pulmonary oedema; other severe pre-eclampsia features; suspected fetal compromise; or other concerning clinical findings.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered repeated comprehensive assessment and admission when wellbeing is at risk appropriate on clinical grounds.

recommendations.statement: Consider fullPIERS or PREP-S to inform the appropriate place of care, including possible in utero transfer, and intervention thresholds.
recommendations.context: Use these models alongside clinical assessment in women with pre-eclampsia.
recommendations.rationale: Some evidence indicated that these models help distinguish maternal risk of adverse outcomes.

recommendations.statement: When applying a risk model, account for fullPIERS being usable at any point in pregnancy, PREP-S being intended only up to 34 weeks, and neither model predicting outcomes for babies.

For pre-eclampsia without severe hypertension, admit if maternal or fetal wellbeing is concerning or fullPIERS or PREP-S indicates high risk; offer medication if BP remains above 140/90 mmHg and target 135/85 mmHg or less. Measure BP at least every 48 hours, more often during admission; repeat dipstick proteinuria testing only when clinically indicated; measure full blood count, liver and renal function twice a week. For severe hypertension, admit and treat all women, managing as hypertension if BP falls below 160/ 110 mmHg; target 135/85 mmHg or less. Measure BP every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110 mmHg, then at least 4 times daily during admission according to clinical circumstances; repeat dipstick testing only when indicated and perform blood tests 3 times a week. In both groups, auscultate the fetal heart at every antenatal visit, perform ultrasound at diagnosis and, if normal, every 2 weeks, and perform CTG at diagnosis and subsequently only if clinically indicated.
recommendations.context: The circumstances warranting repeat dipstick testing include new symptoms or signs or uncertainty about diagnosis.
recommendations.rationale: The committee used maternal and fetal concerns and predicted complication risk to guide admission; evidence directly addressing treatment-initiation and target BP thresholds in pre-eclampsia was unavailable.

recommendations.statement: Offer labetalol for hypertension accompanying pre-eclampsia. Offer nifedipine if labetalol is unsuitable, or methyldopa if labetalol or nifedipine is unsuitable. Consider existing treatment, adverse effects, risks including fetal effects, and the woman's preference.
recommendations.context: At publication, some nifedipine brands were specifically contraindicated during pregnancy in their manufacturers' product information.
recommendations.rationale: Comparative evidence on medicines was insufficient to identify one as superior; the committee retained treatment choices from the previous guideline.

recommendations.statement: Document maternal and fetal thresholds for planned birth before 37 weeks in women with pre-eclampsia. Potential thresholds include BP uncontrolled despite 3 or more appropriately dosed antihypertensive classes; maternal oxygen saturation less than 90%; worsening liver or renal function, haemolysis or platelet count; continuing neurological features such as severe refractory headache, repeated visual scotomata or eclampsia; placental abruption; reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery doppler, a nonreassuring cardiotocograph or stillbirth. Other features may also justify planned early birth.
recommendations.context: Pulse oximeters may under- or overestimate saturation, particularly near a threshold; overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin.
recommendations.rationale: Because evidence comparing early birth with continued pregnancy was limited, the committee based timing on the risks of continuing pregnancy for the woman and baby.

recommendations.statement: Include a senior obstetrician in decisions about when a woman with pre-eclampsia will give birth.
Consult the anaesthetic team when birth is planned for a woman with pre-eclampsia.
Consult the neonatal team when birth is planned for a woman with pre-eclampsia and neonatal complications are expected.

If early birth is planned for preterm pre-eclampsia, offer intravenous magnesium sulfate and a course of antenatal corticosteroids when indicated, in accordance with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth.

Before 34 weeks in pre-eclampsia, continue surveillance unless an indication for planned early birth arises, and offer intravenous magnesium sulfate and antenatal corticosteroids in line with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth. From 34 weeks to 36 weeks plus 6 days, continue surveillance unless early birth is indicated; when considering early birth, assess maternal and fetal condition, risks including maternal comorbidities and multi-fetal pregnancy, and neonatal bed availability, and consider antenatal corticosteroids. From 37 weeks onwards, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours.
recommendations.context: Indications for planned early birth are addressed in the section on timing of birth.
recommendations.rationale: The committee considered continued surveillance to 37 weeks appropriate unless particular concerns warrant earlier birth.

recommendations.statement: After birth in a woman with pre-eclampsia who did not take antihypertensives, measure BP at least 4 times daily during admission, at least once between day 3 and day 5, and on alternate days until normal if it was abnormal on days 3 to 5.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: After birth, start antihypertensive treatment if BP is 150/ 100 mmHg or higher in a woman with pre-eclampsia who did not previously receive it.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: At every postnatal BP check, ask a woman with pre-eclampsia about severe headache and epigastric pain.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: After birth in a woman with pre-eclampsia who received antihypertensives, measure BP at least 4 times daily during admission and every 1 to 2 days for up to 2 weeks after transfer to community care, until she has stopped treatment and no longer has hypertension.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: After birth in a woman treated with antihypertensives for pre-eclampsia, continue treatment; consider reducing it if BP falls below 140/90 mmHg and reduce it if BP falls below 130/ 80 mmHg.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: If methyldopa was used for pre-eclampsia, stop it within 2 days after birth and switch treatment if needed.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: Offer transfer to community care after birth to a woman with pre-eclampsia only when she has no pre-eclampsia symptoms, her BP with or without treatment is 150/100 mmHg or less, and blood test results are stable or improving.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: For a woman transferred to community care after pre-eclampsia, document follow-up responsibility and any needed medical review, BP monitoring frequency, thresholds for reducing or stopping treatment, indications for primary-care BP review, and self-monitoring for symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: Offer a GP or specialist review 2 weeks after transfer to community care to women who have had pre-eclampsia and remain on antihypertensives.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: Offer all women who have had pre-eclampsia a medical review with a GP or specialist 6 to 8 weeks after birth.
recommendations.source_heading: Postnatal investigation, monitoring and treatment (including after discharge from critical care) — Blood pressure

recommendations.statement: In women with pre-eclampsia and mild or moderate hypertension, or after leaving critical care, check platelets, transaminases and serum creatinine 48 to 72 hours after birth or critical-care step-down. Do not repeat these measurements if they are normal at 48 to 72 hours.

After birth, if biochemical or haematological results in a woman with pre-eclampsia remain outside their reference ranges, repeat platelets, transaminases and serum creatinine as clinically indicated until they normalise.
Perform a urine reagent-strip test 6 to 8 weeks after birth in women who have had pre-eclampsia.
If proteinuria remains at 1+ or more at 6 to 8 weeks after birth following pre-eclampsia, offer another GP or specialist review at 3 months after birth to assess kidney function.
Consider specialist kidney assessment for women whose kidney-function assessment is abnormal at 3 months, in accordance with the NICE guideline on chronic kidney disease.
recommendations.context: Follow-up after pre-eclampsia.

recommendations.statement: For chronic hypertension, assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid by ultrasound and perform umbilical artery doppler velocimetry at 28 weeks, 32 weeks and 36 weeks.
In chronic hypertension, perform cardiotocography only when clinically indicated.

In gestational hypertension, assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid by ultrasound and perform umbilical artery doppler velocimetry at diagnosis; if results are normal, repeat every 2 to 4 weeks when clinically indicated.
In gestational hypertension, perform cardiotocography only when clinically indicated.
Perform cardiotocography when pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension is diagnosed.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: If conservative management is planned for pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension, assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid by ultrasound and perform umbilical artery doppler velocimetry at diagnosis.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: If all fetal monitoring results are normal in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension, do not routinely repeat cardiotocography unless clinically indicated.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: Repeat cardiotocography in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension if the woman reports changed fetal movements, vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain, or if her condition deteriorates.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: In pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension, repeat ultrasound assessment of fetal growth and amniotic fluid or umbilical artery doppler velocimetry every 2 weeks, then tailor further surveillance to scan findings.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: For pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension, document the timing and type of subsequent fetal monitoring, fetal indications for birth, whether and when to give antenatal corticosteroids, and plans to consult neonatal paediatricians and obstetric anaesthetists.
recommendations.source_heading: Fetal monitoring in pre-eclampsia or severe gestational hypertension

recommendations.statement: For a woman with previous severe pre-eclampsia, pre-eclampsia leading to birth before 34 weeks, pre-eclampsia with birth weight below the 10th centile, intrauterine death or placental abruption, assess fetal growth and amniotic fluid by ultrasound and perform umbilical artery doppler velocimetry starting between 28 and 30 weeks, or at least 2 weeks before the previous gestational age of onset if that was earlier than 28 weeks, and repeat 4 weeks later.
recommendations.source_heading: Women who need additional fetal monitoring

recommendations.statement: In women requiring additional fetal monitoring because of the specified previous pregnancy complications, perform cardiotocography only when clinically indicated.
recommendations.source_heading: Women who need additional fetal monitoring

recommendations.statement: During labour and birth, provide advice, treatment and care for hypertensive disorders in accordance with the NICE guideline on intrapartum care unless this guideline addresses the same topic. Care should reflect more than labour BP alone and apply whether hypertension is treated or untreated.

Provide women with chronic hypertension intrapartum advice and care consistent with the NICE guideline on intrapartum care for women with existing medical conditions or obstetric complications and their babies.
During labour, check BP hourly in women with hypertension, or every 15 to 30 minutes in women with severe hypertension until BP is less than 160/110 mmHg.
Continue antenatal antihypertensive treatment throughout labour.
During labour, use the antenatal criteria to decide whether women with hypertension need haematological or biochemical tests, even when regional analgesia is being considered.
Do not preload a woman with severe pre-eclampsia with intravenous fluids before initiating low-dose epidural or combined spinal epidural analgesia.
Do not routinely shorten the second stage of labour in women whose hypertension is controlled.
recommendations.source_heading: Management of second stage of labour

recommendations.statement: Consider operative or assisted birth during the second stage for a woman with severe hypertension that has not responded to initial treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: Management of second stage of labour

recommendations.statement: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate to a woman in critical care with severe hypertension or severe pre-eclampsia who has had an eclamptic seizure, whether current or earlier.
Consider intravenous magnesium sulfate for a woman with severe pre-eclampsia in critical care if birth is planned within 24 hours.
